## Overview

> **Writing the code was the easy part. Validating it, maintaining it, and earning the community's trust to become a standard is the ongoing work this proposal supports.**

Since our previous submission, `OptSurvCutR` has been accepted onto CRAN (v0.10, and now v0.11.1). It was not yet on CRAN at the time of that submission and has since had a post-acceptance maintenance release. This proposal funds the next phase: completing and reporting a simulation study that empirically tests the package's central stability claim; using that study to finish an already-planned update of the bioRxiv preprint [@yau2025preprint] ahead of submission to *BMC Bioinformatics*; and, alongside completing `rOpenSci` review, building an accessible entry point for researchers who are not R specialists.

The benefit to the R community is filling a real gap in the survival-analysis ecosystem: existing cut-point packages (@sec-problem) find a significant threshold but do not test its reproducibility as standard practice. Closing that gap in one well-supported package, rather than leaving it to individual users to notice, benefits every downstream user of prognostic biomarker analysis in R.

The plan runs over six months in three milestones, detailed in @sec-timeline.

Full detail in @sec-timeline.

### Minimum Viable Product

The smallest complete deliverable is the simulation study: data simulated under known one-cut and two-cut ground truths, testing whether the stability tiers predict recovery of the true threshold out of sample.

The manuscript is explicit about why this matters. It states that bootstrap resampling does not establish that a threshold will be recovered in an independent population, that this relationship has not been evaluated, and that the tier boundaries of 30% and 60% are "pragmatic conventions rather than calibrated thresholds." The simulation study is designed to test exactly that.

### Architecture

Both deliverables sit on top of the existing package: the simulation study is a self-contained Quarto document that tests its outputs against known ground truth, and the script wraps `find_cutpoint_number()`, `find_cutpoint()` and `validate_cutpoint()` without changing the statistical engines.

### Assumptions

- The simulation study completes on the stated timeline once started; if the tier system does not calibrate as hypothesised, that is reported as a genuine finding in the preprint update, not concealed.
- *BMC Bioinformatics* review proceeds on a normal journal timeline; submission itself is within this project's control, acceptance is not, and the corresponding milestone is scoped to "submitted," not "accepted."
- The target user for the clinician-facing script can run an R script but does not want to learn the package's full function-level API. If this assumption is wrong, the script's value is much smaller, and that milestone should be re-scoped toward documentation instead.
- `rOpenSci` review continues on a timeline compatible with the proposal window; if review stalls for reasons outside this project's control, that milestone may need to report progress rather than completion.

### External dependencies

`survival`, `survminer`, `rgenoud`, `Rcpp`, `ggplot2`, `patchwork`, `cli`, `tidyr`, `rlang`, `foreach`, `doParallel` and `doRNG` (the package's Imports at v0.11.1; see DESCRIPTION); no new external dependencies are anticipated for the simulation study or the clinician-facing script. `rOpenSci` review timing is an external dependency outside this project's direct control (see Assumptions, above).
